questions.q: What does SQL Server's IDENTITY(1, 1) column property mean?
options: It requires a separate SEQUENCE object to function
The column can only ever hold the value 1
It is identical to MySQL's AUTO_INCREMENT in exact syntax, just a different keyword
A seed of 1 and an increment of 1 -- the database generates and tracks the next sequential value automatically
questions.explain: IDENTITY(seed, increment) auto-generates values starting at the seed and increasing by the increment each time.

questions.q: What is Oracle's traditional approach to auto-incrementing a primary key, before 12c's IDENTITY syntax existed?
options: A single column attribute called AUTO_INCREMENT, same as MySQL
Create a SEQUENCE object, then a BEFORE INSERT trigger that pulls the next sequence value into the column
Oracle has always had a direct IDENTITY column property, identical to SQL Server
There was no way to auto-increment a key in Oracle before 12c
questions.explain: The traditional Oracle pattern pairs a SEQUENCE object with a trigger to populate the column on insert.

questions.q: What does PostgreSQL's SERIAL pseudo-type actually create behind the scenes?
options: A SEQUENCE object, which SERIAL is really just shorthand for
A native boolean type
A trigger identical to Oracle's traditional pattern, with no sequence involved
A CHECK constraint with no underlying object
questions.explain: SERIAL/BIGSERIAL are convenience shorthand that create a real SEQUENCE object automatically.

questions.q: How does Oracle's modern (12c+) IDENTITY column syntax relate to its traditional approach?
options: It completely replaces sequences and has nothing to do with them internally
It's built on a sequence under the hood, with the trigger machinery handled automatically instead of written by hand
It is unrelated to SEQUENCE and uses a totally different internal mechanism
It only works for VARCHAR2 columns, not numeric ones
questions.explain: Oracle's modern IDENTITY syntax is still sequence-based internally -- it just hides the sequence-plus-trigger boilerplate from the developer.

questions.q: Which platform uses a single, direct column attribute with no separate object involved for auto-incrementing keys?
options: PostgreSQL, with SERIAL always requiring a manually created SEQUENCE
Oracle, with its traditional SEQUENCE and trigger pattern
MySQL, with AUTO_INCREMENT directly on the column
SQL Server, which requires a separate SEQUENCE object for every table
questions.explain: MySQL's AUTO_INCREMENT is the most direct of the four -- a column attribute with no separate sequence object to manage.
